subtype: Approach: spending on snacks and forgetting the goal [Pitfall]
passage:
Week one, Monday. Avni got money from Papa and put half in the jar. On the way home, Avni bought chips and a packet of stickers with the rest. It was only a little, Avni told herself.

Week three, Thursday. The jar felt light. Avni shook it and counted eight coins. There had been chips on Tuesday, a sticker book on Friday, and a lollipop today. Nobody had counted any of it.

Week five, Saturday. Avni opened the jar and found almost nothing. The toy in the shop window was as far away as on the first day.

qa.q: What did Avni buy on the way home in the first week?
qa.a: Avni bought chips and a packet of stickers.

qa.q: What might Avni be feeling when opening the jar in week five?
qa.a: Avni is probably disappointed and surprised, since the jar is almost empty and the toy still feels far away. 😔

qa.q: What alternative approach could Avni use, and why?
qa.a: Avni could write down each spend and set aside the savings first, before buying snacks. Counting small spends shows where the money goes.

qa.q: How might Papa see the empty jar?
qa.a: Papa gave the money each week and would probably see how easily small spends add up, and may want to help Avni set a fixed amount aside.

grounding: A child buys chips and stickers with weekly money, and after a month the jar is nearly empty because the small spends were never counted.

subtype: Approach: spending on snacks and forgetting the goal [Pitfall]
passage: Mehak, you want to know why I always ask where your pocket money goes? When your Dadu Pradeep was nine, I wanted a real cricket bat, the willow kind. Every Monday my father gave me a few coins, and every Monday I said, 'This goes in the tin.' But the shop near school sold salted chips in paper cones, and cricket stickers in little packets. One cone, one packet, it felt like nothing. After a month I shook the tin. Two coins rattled inside. I sat on the floor and counted every cone I could remember. It was the bat, all of it, gone into my stomach and my sticker book.

qa.q: What did the shop near school sell?
qa.a: Salted chips in paper cones and cricket stickers in little packets.

qa.q: How might young Pradeep have felt when he shook the tin?
qa.a: He probably felt shocked and disappointed, hearing only two coins after a month.

qa.q: What choice in the story could have kept the money for the bat?
qa.a: Putting the coins in the tin before passing the shop, or noting each small spend so he'd see them adding up.

qa.q: How might Pradeep's father have seen the empty tin?
qa.a: His father had given coins every Monday, so he might have felt disappointed, or hoped his son would learn from counting the cones.

grounding: Shows a child spending weekly money on chips and stickers at the shop near school until, after a month, the tin is nearly empty.

subtype: Approach: spending on snacks and forgetting the goal [Pitfall]
passage: All through May the heat was terrible, and the shop right outside the school gate had a freezer of ice lollies and a rack of glitter stickers. Lavanya was saving for a set of watercolours. Every Monday Amma gave her pocket money, and every Monday she promised herself it was going straight into the jar. But at 3 pm, sticky and hot, Parul would say, 'One lolly?' and Lavanya would think, just this once. Stickers on Wednesday. Chips on Friday. She never wrote any of it down. On the last day of the month she tipped the jar out on her bed. Three coins. She stared at them, then at the empty space on her shelf where the paint box was meant to go.

qa.q: How did Lavanya feel when she tipped out the jar?
qa.a: She stared at the three coins, so she felt shocked and disappointed that the small spends had eaten her savings.

qa.q: What could Lavanya try next month?
qa.a: Put the money in the jar the moment Amma gives it and note any spend, perhaps with Amma's help, so small treats don't go unnoticed.

qa.q: How might Parul see her 'One lolly?' now?
qa.a: Parul only meant to share a treat in the heat and may not have known Lavanya was saving, so she might feel sorry if she found out.

grounding: Illustrates a child buying lollies, stickers and chips near school each week without counting, and finding the savings jar nearly empty after a month.
